title: Suncorp’s Townsville hub brings claims operations closer to North Queensland
full_text:
Suncorp has marked the first anniversary of its Townsville Regional Hub, reporting the facility has created more than 120 local jobs and now handles claims and customer service for policyholders across North Queensland.
The hub, opened in mid-2025, houses customer service, claims, compulsory third party (CTP), national assessing, operational excellence, and brand and customer experience teams. Staff cover the AAMI, Suncorp, GIO, and Apia brands. New recruits go through multi-week, cohort-based in-person training.
The Townsville facility also functions as a satellite disaster response hub, integrated with Suncorp’s Disaster Management Centre in Brisbane. A Mobile Disaster Response Hub, known internally as “Larry,” is permanently stationed there for deployment during declared weather events.
North Queensland’s natural peril exposure gives that model its commercial logic. The February 2025 floods generated 11,770 claims and $316 million in insured losses, according to the Insurance Council of Australia (ICA). Ex-Tropical Cyclone Alfred followed weeks later.
The contrast with how Australia’s other major personal lines insurer approaches the same region is instructive. IAG – whose brands include NRMA Insurance, CGU, and WFI – operates a 24/7 Major Event Response Team and a Natural Perils Team that monitors weather events and mobilises to affected communities once conditions allow.
During the February 2025 North Queensland floods, IAG deployed claims specialists to Townsville Sports Stadium and sent assessors and partner builders into Ingham for property inspections and emergency make-safe repairs, according to IAG’s own statements.
The distinction, based on each company’s publicly documented approach, is between a permanently staffed regional presence and a specialist team deployed from elsewhere when events occur. No independent assessment has compared claims resolution times or dispute rates between the two models in the same geography.

Suncorp regional customer manager Mark Hamblyn said the hub was designed so locally based staff handle customers in a region with concentrated weather risk. “We’ve built a highly capable workforce that now supports customers across AAMI, Suncorp, GIO, and Apia, while helping us strengthen our connection to North Queensland communities,” Hamblyn said.
AAMI specialist Kenny Mathie, among the first cohort hired when the hub opened, said local presence changes how customers respond. “If someone asks where I’m based, I can tell them I’m right around the corner in Townsville. They often assume we’re in one of the bigger cities, so knowing they’ve reached someone local who’s experienced the same weather events helps build trust and connection,” Mathie said.
Suncorp/GIO specialist Marianne Baylon said internal knowledge-sharing helps when unfamiliar claim scenarios arise. “When I encounter a situation I haven’t experienced before, there’s always someone willing to guide me or point me in the right direction. That shared expertise helps me provide customers with more confident, accurate, and efficient support,” Baylon said.
These are accounts from Suncorp employees. No independent assessment of the hub’s effect on claims outcomes has been published.
Claims handling has become more publicly measurable in the year since the hub opened. The Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) recorded 36,022 general insurance complaints in 2025-26, up 5% on the prior year, with delay in claim handling the top issue across all financial products. The General Insurance Code Governance Committee’s 2024-25 Industry Data and Compliance Report found 70,325 code breaches across the industry – up 20.5% – with claims-related failures accounting for 59% of the total. More than half of the insurers that breached key claims-handling timeframes could not say by how many days they had kept customers waiting.
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) listed claims and complaint handling as a 2026 enforcement priority.

In March 2026, ASIC launched its Internal Dispute Resolution (IDR) data dashboard, enabling firm-level comparison of complaint volumes and resolution times across general insurers for the first time. Location data is excluded from firm-level publication, so no Queensland-specific breakdown is available for any insurer.
Hamblyn, who relocated from Adelaide after 14 years with Suncorp and took over day-to-day leadership after founding manager Kelly Green went on parental leave, said the first year centred on operational stability. “The ability to maintain such a high level of engagement in our team while establishing stability at a new site is a personal highlight for me,” he said.
Suncorp CEO Steve Johnston flagged in the group’s FY26 results that strategic focus is turning to “the way we manage claims.”
Hamblyn said year two is about depth. “Now the opportunity is to deepen our connections in the community, continue developing local talent, and ensure every customer interaction reflects the passion and commitment our team brings every day,” he said.
For brokers placing risks in North Queensland, the operative question – whether a permanent regional presence produces different claims outcomes than event-activated deployment – remains unanswered by available public data. AFCA’s monthly Datacube updates and Suncorp’s coming half-year results are the nearest data points for tracking whether that changes.
